content.title: Evaluating Evidence for Scientific Claims
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the ability to determine whether specific experimental data supports, weakens, or is irrelevant to a scientific claim by comparing predicted effects with observed outcomes.
learning_objectives: Identify the specific predicted relationship and variables within a scientific claim.
Evaluate whether experimental conditions and measured outcomes align with a claim.
Determine if data supports or weakens a claim based on the direction and magnitude of the results.

sections.title: The Components of Evidence Evaluation
sections.content:
To evaluate evidence, you must break a claim down into three parts: the manipulated variable (the cause), the measured outcome (the effect), and the predicted direction of change. Evidence supports a claim if the manipulated variable leads to the predicted change in the outcome. Evidence weakens a claim if the manipulated variable leads to no change or the opposite change. Evidence is irrelevant if it measures a different variable or uses conditions that do not match the claim's context.

![A flowchart showing the steps to evaluate if evidence supports or weakens a claim.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/67a60b39-1992-4347-946b-2551c3da656e-1786506706881-458.webp)

sections.title: Supporting vs. Weakening Evidence
sections.content: Support occurs when the data shows a clear trend that matches the hypothesis (e.g., if the claim says 'Temperature increases growth,' the data should show higher growth at higher temperatures). Weakening occurs when the data contradicts the hypothesis (e.g., growth stays the same or decreases as temperature rises). When comparing multiple datasets, the strongest evidence usually comes from trials that directly isolate the variables mentioned in the claim without introducing confounding factors.

worked_examples.question: Claim: 'Adding Compound X to soil increases seedling height.' Study Results: (A) Low sunlight, X vs. no X: 5.1 cm vs. 5.0 cm. (B) Greenhouse, X vs. no X: 7.8 cm vs. 5.2 cm. (C) Compound Y increases height to 6.0 cm. Which result most weakens the claim?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the claim—Compound X should cause an increase in height. Step 2: Analyze Result A—It compares X to no X but shows almost no difference (0.1 cm), which contradicts the 'increase' prediction. Step 3: Analyze Result B—This supports the claim. Step 4: Analyze Result C—This is irrelevant because it tests Compound Y, not X. Conclusion: Result A most weakens the claim because it directly tests the variable and fails to show the predicted effect.

common_mistakes: Choosing irrelevant data that involves different variables than those in the claim.
Confusing a 'lack of change' with 'support' just because the values are high.
Ignoring the control group (the 'no treatment' group) when determining if a change actually occurred.
exam_tips: Always look for the 'control' or 'baseline' data to see what the 'normal' state is before the variable was changed.
Check the units and scale; a very small numerical difference might be statistically insignificant and thus weaken a claim of a 'major' effect.
If a question asks what 'weakens' a claim, look for the data point that shows the opposite of the predicted trend.
content.recap: Evaluating evidence requires matching the claim's variables to the study's results. Data supports a claim if the outcome matches the predicted direction and weakens it if the outcome is stagnant or moves in the opposite direction.

knowledge_claims.content: A scientific claim is a predicted relationship between a manipulated variable and a measured outcome.
To evaluate evidence, first identify the specific predicted effect and the key variable being manipulated.
Evidence supports a claim if the observed outcome matches the direction and size of the predicted effect.
Evidence weakens a claim if the observed outcome shows no change or a change opposite to what was predicted.
Data is considered irrelevant to a claim if it measures a different variable than the one specified in the claim.
When evaluating evidence, confirm that the study's conditions (like temperature or light) match the context of the claim.
A common mistake is selecting evidence that shows a high value but lacks a comparison to a control group.
Strong evidence requires comparing a treatment group (with the manipulated variable) against a control group (without it).
A result showing 5.1 cm vs 5.0 cm in a growth study indicates a negligible difference that likely weakens a claim of significant growth.
If a claim states 'Variable A decreases Variable B,' evidence showing B increasing when A is added weakens the claim.
Reject results as evidence if they involve confounded setups where multiple variables are changed simultaneously.
The magnitude of change in the data must be sufficient to support the claim's specific wording (e.g., 'significant increase').

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 3: Paper Rotor Descent
A class built paper rotors with two folded blades. Experiment 1 compared blade lengths while rotor mass was held constant. Experiment 2 added paper clips to the medium-blade rotor. Students released each rotor from the same height indoors and recorded mean descent time.

Which conclusion is best supported by the combined experiments?
F) The experiment proves the pattern will remain unchanged under every possible condition.
G) The independent variable had no relationship to any measured outcome.
H) Longer blades increased descent time, whereas adding mass to the medium rotor decreased it.
J) The data justify replacing all observations with a single average.

options.A: The experiment proves the pattern will remain unchanged under every possible condition.
options.B: The independent variable had no relationship to any measured outcome.
options.C: Longer blades increased descent time, whereas adding mass to the medium rotor decreased it.
options.D: The data justify replacing all observations with a single average.

items.explanation: The conclusion reflects the measured results and remains within the experimental scope.

items.stem:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 4: Stream Turbidity After Rain
A watershed team measured turbidity at an upstream forest site and a downstream roadside site before rainfall and at three times after a storm. Higher turbidity means that more suspended particles scatter light.

Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
F) Turbidity rose at both sites after rain, with a larger and more persistent increase at the roadside site.
G) Every value in both series was identical.
H) The measured outcome changed randomly with no visible pattern.
J) The results prove the same pattern must occur under all untested conditions.

options.A: Turbidity rose at both sites after rain, with a larger and more persistent increase at the roadside site.
options.B: Every value in both series was identical.
options.C: The measured outcome changed randomly with no visible pattern.
options.D: The results prove the same pattern must occur under all untested conditions.

items.explanation: The conclusion accurately summarizes the plotted pattern without extending beyond the tested conditions.

videoLesson.title: Select Evidence That Supports Or Weakens
videoLesson.description: Recognize whether outcomes match the claim's predicted effect and key manipulated variables. Compare conditions and decide if the reported evidence supports, contradicts, or is irrelevant to the claim.
